title: Drug-Resistant Infections Kill Up to Half of ICU Patients in Indian Hospitals, Landmark ICMR Study Finds
excerpt: A three-year study of 159,336 patients across 20 hospitals reveals that carbapenem-resistant bacteria drive sharply higher mortality and treatment costs, with most infections acquired inside healthcare facilities.
body:
• A landmark ICMR study of 159,336 hospitalized patients across 20 Indian hospitals found that over 60% of Gram-negative infections were resistant to carbapenem antibiotics — the last line of defense.
  • Mortality in bloodstream infections caused by carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter and Pseudomonas reached 46–51%, with treatment costs 1.1 to 2 times higher than for susceptible infections.
  • More than 85% of drug-resistant infections were healthcare-associated, pointing to hospital infection control as a critical intervention point.
  • The study, published in The Lancet Regional Health – Southeast Asia, is one of the first to link India's AMR surveillance data directly to patient outcomes and costs.

The Scale of the Crisis

A three-year multi-centre study tracking over 150,000 hospitalized patients across 20 Indian tertiary-care hospitals has quantified what infectious disease specialists have long warned: when common bacteria outsmart last-resort antibiotics, patients die at sharply higher rates and treatment costs spiral.

Published in The Lancet Regional Health – Southeast Asia (Volume 53, October 2026), the study was led by Dr. Kamini Walia of the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), who heads its Descriptive Research Division and leads India's antimicrobial resistance surveillance program. The research team analyzed data from April 2022 to April 2025, covering more than 1.75 million patient-days of care.

Of 159,336 patients studied, 27,283 had microbiologically confirmed infections. Among the 26,213 with Gram-negative bacterial infections — including E. coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa — more than six in ten were resistant to carbapenem antibiotics.

Death Rates Surge With Resistance

Across all four major pathogens, carbapenem-resistant infections carried significantly higher mortality. Patients with resistant E. coli faced a 41% higher relative risk of death; for Pseudomonas aeruginosa, the increase was 43%. Klebsiella pneumoniae showed 33% higher risk, and Acinetobacter baumannii 16%.

The absolute numbers are stark. Mortality hit 24.4% for carbapenem-resistant E. coli versus 17.3% for susceptible infections. For Klebsiella, it was 31.2% versus 23.5%. Acinetobacter had the highest overall mortality at 37.9% for resistant strains.

The most alarming figures emerged from bloodstream infections. Carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter and Pseudomonas caused mortality rates between 46% and 51% — nearly one in two patients.

"Carbapenem drug-resistant infections caused substantially higher mortality and treatment costs than susceptible infections. For India, the study highlights the need to move beyond drug resistance surveillance to integrated surveillance linking AMR with patient outcomes."

— Dr. Kamini Walia, Senior Scientist, ICMR

The Financial Toll

Drug resistance carries a steep economic penalty. Antibiotic treatment costs for resistant infections ran 1.1 to 2 times higher than for susceptible ones. When first-line drugs fail, clinicians must turn to newer, more expensive agents like ceftazidime-avibactam or complex drug combinations, often requiring longer hospital stays and intensive monitoring.

Patients with carbapenem-resistant E. coli averaged 23-day hospital stays, compared to 18 days for susceptible infections. A grim paradox emerged with Acinetobacter and Pseudomonas: hospital stays were sometimes shorter for resistant cases — because patients died sooner.

Hospitals Are the Epicenter

The study's most actionable finding may be its sourcing data. Healthcare-associated infections accounted for 85% of E. coli cases, 91.6% of Klebsiella cases, 91.9% of Pseudomonas cases, and 95.1% of Acinetobacter cases. The vast majority of drug-resistant infections were acquired inside medical facilities, not in the community.

This concentration points to infection prevention — hand hygiene, environmental cleaning, proper management of invasive devices, rapid identification of resistant organisms — as the most direct lever for reducing the burden.

What It Means for India's Health System

The study is significant because it goes beyond laboratory surveillance to measure real-world outcomes. Previous Indian AMR data could show that bacteria were resistant to specific drugs, but not what that resistance meant for patients in terms of survival and cost. This research closes that gap across a nationally representative sample.

The authors caution that their participating hospitals have high standards of infection control and lab support. "We suspect that hospitals with poor laboratory support to facilitate timely identification and treatment may have far worse patient outcomes compared to what is documented in this study," they write.

For India's broader public health infrastructure, the message is direct: antimicrobial stewardship — prescribing the right drug at the right dose for the right duration — is no longer optional. Neither is investing in rapid diagnostics and newer effective antibiotics. Preventing resistance costs far less than trying to outrun it.
nri_angle: NRIs seeking hospital care in India should be aware of antimicrobial resistance risks, particularly in ICU settings, and ask about infection-control protocols.
